questions.question: What are a few simple design patterns useful in Ruby?
questions.title: Simple Design Patterns in Ruby
questions.direct_answer: Design patterns are named solutions to common problems. A few useful in Ruby: Singleton (one instance of a class — Ruby has Singleton module), Factory (a method that builds the right object based on input, hiding the class choice), Adapter (wrap an external API so your code calls one interface), Decorator (add behavior to an object without changing its class, e.g. a presenter), Observer (notify listeners on an event — ActiveSupport::Notifications). They're vocabulary, not a mandate; use them when the problem genuinely fits, and prefer Ruby's blocks/modules over heavy class hierarchies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name a few patterns (Singleton/Factory/Adapter/Decorator/Observer) and know Ruby's lighter take (modules, blocks).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forcing a pattern where a simple method would do (over-engineering), or the Singleton-module confusion with the GoF singleton-by-hand.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Patterns are named solutions: Singleton, Factory, Adapter, Decorator, Observer. Use when the problem fits; prefer Ruby's modules/blocks over heavy hierarchies.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Design patterns are named solutions to common problems. A few useful in Ruby: Singleton — one instance of a class, and Ruby has a Singleton module for it; Factory — a method that builds the right object based on input, hiding the class choice; Adapter — wrap an external API so your code calls one consistent interface; Decorator — add behavior to an object without changing its class, like a presenter that adds formatted methods to a model; Observer — notify listeners on an event, via ActiveSupport colon colon Notifications. They're vocabulary, not a mandate; use them when the problem genuinely fits, and prefer Ruby's blocks and modules over heavy class hierarchies, because Ruby's flexibility often makes the lightweight version cleaner than the textbook one. A common mistake is forcing a pattern where a simple method would do, which is over-engineering, and building heavy class hierarchies when a module or block is cleaner in Ruby.

sections.title: Pattern -> Use
sections.content:
Pick the pattern that fits; prefer Ruby's light version.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[problem] -->|one instance| S[Singleton]
  P -->|pick class by input| F[Factory]
  P -->|unify an API| A[Adapter]
  P -->|add behavior| D[Decorator]
  P -->|notify on event| O[Observer]
```

sections.title: Simple patterns
sections.content:
```ruby
# Singleton (Ruby's Singleton module)
require 'singleton'
class AppConfig
  include Singleton
  attr_accessor :env
end
AppConfig.instance.env = 'prod'   # one shared instance

# Factory: pick the class by input
class PaymentFactory
  def self.for(kind)
    case kind
    when 'stripe' then StripePayment
    when 'paypal' then PaypalPayment
    else raise "unknown #{kind}"
    end
  end
end
PaymentFactory.for('stripe').new.charge(100)

# Decorator (presenter): add formatted methods without changing the model
class UserPresenter
  def initialize(user); @user = user; end
  def full_name; "#{@user.first} #{@user.last}"; end
  def initials; @user.first[0] + @user.last[0]; end
end
```
